description: Official US facts about an address or point: FEMA's flood zone at that exact spot (with what the zone means and whether lenders require flood insurance), FEMA National Risk Index ratings for the census tract across 18 natural hazards (flooding, hurricane, wildfire, tornado, earthquake, heat and more), active National Weather Service alerts, current air quality with a 2-day forecast (EPA AirNow), the state's average home electricity price against the US average (EIA), and the county's internet providers with the share of homes each reports it can serve (FCC National Broadband Map), federal disaster declarations and earthquakes nearby, how home prices moved in the metro or state over 1, 5 and 10 years (FHFA House Price Index), public EV chargers within 2 miles and the electric utility (DOE), reported violent and property crime per 100,000 for the city's police or county sheriff against the state and US (FBI), the county's adult health estimates such as obesity, diabetes, smoking and uninsured rates (CDC PLACES), the public water system serving the point with its Safe Drinking Water Act violations over the last 3 years (EPA), and the nearest free HUD-approved housing counselors, and the county's childcare prices by age (US Department of Labor). Use when someone is buying, renting or moving somewhere, or asks about flood or disaster risk for a US address. Send a full street address, or latitude and longitude for a city or ZIP. Outside the US, send latitude and longitude: divux returns earthquakes, active disaster alerts within 500 km (GDACS) and the 10-day weather risk; the rest is US data. Not an insurance quote or a guarantee.Parks (park): a US national park, monument or historic site from the National Park Service: current alerts and closures, entrance fees, hours and today's exceptions, and campgrounds with Recreation.gov links. Night sky (sky: true, with a point): the chance of seeing the aurora (NOAA's live model and Kp forecast), the moon's phase, sunrise, sunset and full darkness, and on US coasts the next high and low tides. Schools (schools: true, with an address or a point): US public schools closest first from the National Center for Education Statistics: grades, enrollment, students per teacher, share on free or reduced-price lunch, charter status, distance and NCES page; optionally a level and radius. It doesn't say which school is assigned to an address, and has no test scores. Colleges (college): what a US college costs after financial aid and what it leads to, from the Department of Education's College Scorecard: average net price (and by family income), tuition, admission and graduation rates, median debt and median earnings ten years after starting; with a major, that program's graduate earnings and loans. Never call a school good or bad; give the numbers. Send only the parts needed; with schools, sky or college and only a point, the address facts are skipped.

address.description: US street address with city and state, e.g. '1600 Pennsylvania Ave NW, Washington, DC 20500'

college.description: A US college's name, e.g. 'University of Washington', 'Rice University'

lat.description: Latitude, when there's no street address (e.g. the center of a ZIP or city)

major.description: A field of study at the college, for what its graduates earn and borrow, e.g. 'nursing'

park.description: A US national park or site's name or 4-letter NPS code, e.g. 'Yosemite', 'mora'

place.description: Name of the place, for the answer

schools.description: true for public schools near the address or point, closest first

sky.description: true for the night sky at the point: aurora chance, moon, darkness and, on US coasts, tides

state.description: Two-letter state to narrow a common college name, e.g. 'WA'

name: check_place
title: Place check: hazards, weather, schools, parks and the night sky
